first said when it says changed task, it should state what actually changed

the cause, measured, and how I fix it

Built, and in the copy planner. You un-parked it on 13 Nov: “the undo section doesn’t say what changed it just says changed a task it needs to be specific.”

There were TWO faults, and the first one surprised me. Opening a task and pressing Save without editing anything was writing a row into your Undo list. Measured, not guessed: the Repeat control fills in a blank value as it builds, which counts as a change to the stored data — so the planner dutifully recorded it, and since nothing you did had a name, the row read Changed a task. That is where most of those rows in your picture came from.

beforeafter
open a task, press Save, change nothinga row appears: Changed a taskno row at all

The second fault: the describer only understood a handful of fields. I ran your planner’s own describing code over thirteen kinds of change, before and after:

what you doyour build saysthe new build says
change a task’s durationduration 60 min → 90 minsame — already worked
rename a taskRenamed Call the accountant → Call the bookkeepersame
delete or add a tasknames itsame
tick a task offdone empty → yessame
move a taskChanged a taskMoved “Call the accountant” under “Work”
rename an areaChanged a taskRenamed the area Work → Personal
tally a habitChanged a taskWalk — tally 3 → 4
write in the journalChanged a taskEdited the journal on 2026-11-10
edit a noteChanged a taskEdited a note
add to a listChanged a taskShopping — items milk → milk, eggs
a sync arrives from your phoneChanged a taskSynced with your other devices
change a repeat, tags, colour, block…Changed a tasknamed, with the old and new value

Seven of thirteen were useless. Now it is nought of thirteen.

Why it was broken. Your planner already had a describer, good at tasks — built in September for this same complaint. But it only ever looked at the task tree, while an Undo entry is recorded for every save. So a change anywhere else — areas, habits, the journal, notes, lists — had nothing to describe it. A move fell through too, because moving a task changes none of its fields, only its place.

And one more thing you will see. The text used to be cut off where the new value starts — “Call the accountant — priority empty…” hid the word that matters. Undo rows now wrap onto a second line. Only Undo: Past due, Completed and Deleted hold task names, where one line is right, and you asked me to leave those alone.

Built, and in the copy planner. You un-parked it on 13 Nov: “the red square needs to have another red square to indicate it has a subtask.”

First, something I measured that makes this more worth doing than I thought. A row with subtasks and a row without were drawing the same square — identical size, identical colour, identical border. Not similar: the same.

rowwhat it draws today
a task with subtasks16×16, 1.5px solid red
a task with none16×16, 1.5px solid red — indistinguishable

So there was genuinely no way to tell, which is exactly what you said.

What the marker is today. A hollow red square that gets smaller the deeper a row sits, so depth is already readable at a glance:

  Business  — 10px, top level
      Willingboro 2k  — 8px
          Taxes - 13K  — 6px

Now a task with subtasks carries a second square inside the first, so you can tell without unfolding anything that there is more underneath.

The small-size problem you would have hit, solved by measuring. I said on 11 Nov that this might not work at depth 3, where the square is only a few pixels, and that I would show you two options. In the end neither was needed: the inner square is sized as a percentage of the outer one, so it shrinks with it and keeps a visible gap at every depth. No extra rule, no markers made bigger, nothing to choose.

It is drawn in CSS on the shape your planner already uses for a row with children, so it cannot fall out of step with the tree — there is no list to keep updated and no code that could miss a row.

Both came from acting on what I expected instead of measuring what is there. When you ask "is that Claude or Minimax" — it is me. Minimax writes only the exact text I dictate.
  7. Your list goes up here first. Every item you raise becomes a card with a BEFORE picture, an AFTER picture and how I would fix it. Nothing is written into the planner before that.
  8. No code before you approve the card. You approve card by card. Only when you say “make it live” do I write anything.

  11. Your words are kept, all of them — one line per thing you said. Your first quote stays at the top of the card forever; every later correction is its own dated line underneath, never merged into a paragraph, so you can check each one off. I never replace what you said with my summary.
  12. The AFTER is not one picture — it explains the new setup, step by step, in different pictures. What happens first, what happens next, what it looks like when it works. Never the same picture twice. If nothing is built yet, the card says so in plain words instead of pretending.
  13. Every question sits inside the problem it belongs to — never collected somewhere else. You read one card and answer it there.
  14. I raise what you have not thought of. Every card carries an I also thought of note: the thing your request does not decide — the crowded case, the phone, what happens to what you already have.
  15. I test it in Safari myself — before I call it done, and again after it goes live.
